posts.quote: Trick-or-treat hours are 5 to 7. My porch light hours are 5:01 to 5:02.
posts.caption: Last year I bought four bags of the good candy. Full size, the kind that makes kids yell thank you from the sidewalk. Eleven kids came. Eleven. I was eating peanut butter cups for breakfast until Thanksgiving. So this year I have a system. The light goes on at 5:00 sharp, which is technically participating. It goes off at 5:02, which is technically my right as a homeowner. Anyone who shows up in those two minutes gets a handful and my blessing. Everyone else gets a dark porch and a lesson about punctuality. The candy stays with me. It always does.
posts.first: My neighbor across the street does a whole fog machine and a talking skeleton every year. Kids line up past his mailbox. Last Halloween one of them walked up my steps, looked at my dark porch, and said 'she's probably asleep.' He wasn't wrong. I was in the chair with the bowl.

posts.quote: I asked for the senior discount as a joke. The cashier didn't laugh. She just rang it up.
posts.caption: Thursday at the Kroger on Maple, 4:40 in the afternoon. I'd had a long day and I was feeling funny, so when the cashier asked if I had a rewards card I said no, but I'll take the senior discount. I waited for the laugh. I had the follow-up ready and everything. She didn't even look up. She just pushed a button, said 'there you go, hon,' and handed me a receipt that was eight percent cheaper than my dignity. I said thank you. What else do you say. I went out to the car and checked the mirror for a long time.
posts.first: I told my sister about it on the phone that night, expecting sympathy. She laughed so hard she had to put the phone down. Then she asked which Kroger. She wants to try it Saturday. I told her it works. That's the whole problem.

posts.quote: If you're going to be late, at least have the decency to bring a good story. 'Traffic' is not a story.
posts.caption: Friday, 7:00, the Italian place by the hardware store. I was there at 6:55 because I was raised right. By 7:20 I had finished half the breadbasket and made eye contact with the waiter three separate times. At 7:24 she walks in, unwinds a scarf for what felt like a full minute, and says traffic. Traffic. On a Friday. In a town with four stoplights. I've known this woman since 1989 and I love her, but I need more than that. Give me a flat tire. Give me a raccoon in the garage. Give me a man at the gas station who wouldn't stop talking about his boat. I'll forgive a good story. I'll even buy the dessert.
posts.first: For the record, she did try again the next time. Forty minutes late, and she said a goose was standing in the middle of her driveway and refused to move. I have no idea if that's true. I don't care. That's a story. I ordered her the tiramisu.

posts.quote: I’ve reached the wonderful stage of life where I sleep when I’m tired, laugh when I feel like it, eat dessert first, wear silly slippers with pride, and treat peace and quiet as my biggest luxury. If that bothers anyone, they’ll just have to be bothered on their own.
posts.caption: Sunday at 9:40 in the morning I ate a slice of chocolate cake in my bunny slippers and nobody stopped me. That's the whole story, really, but let me set the scene. The cat was asleep on the rug. The house was so quiet I could hear the clock in the hallway. My phone buzzed twice and I let it. There was a time I'd have been showered, dressed, and halfway through somebody else's to-do list by then. That woman got a lot done. She also never once had cake before lunch. I think about her sometimes. Then I take another bite.
posts.first: My son stopped by unannounced around noon and found me in the same chair, same slippers, second slice. He asked if I was feeling okay. I said I've never felt better in my life. He looked at the slippers for a long time. Then he cut himself a piece and sat down on the couch.

posts.quote: Netflix keeps asking if I'm still watching. I've been on this couch since Saturday. At this point I'm part of the upholstery.
posts.first: The little screen came up at 11:40 last night, right in the middle of an episode about a baking contest I'd already seen. I pressed continue without even looking. My hand just knows where the button is now. My husband said that's not a good sign. I pressed continue on him too.

posts.quote: My financial advisor asked about my long-term goals. I said a recliner by a window and a mailbox with no bills in it. He wrote down 'unclear.'
posts.caption: We meet once a year in his office, the one with the big leather chairs and the bowl of mints nobody eats. He had a whole slideshow this time. Charts, a line going up, a little cartoon of a sailboat. Then he folded his hands and asked what I see for myself in twenty years. I told him the truth. A comfortable recliner that faces a window. A mailbox that only has catalogs in it. Maybe a cat, if one shows up. He looked at me for a second and then wrote one word on his legal pad. I read it upside down. I've been called worse.
posts.first: On my way out, his assistant asked if I wanted to schedule next year. I said sure, same time, and asked if the mints were real. She said they've been there since she started. I took one anyway. It was fine. Some things just last if you leave them alone.

posts.quote: My car makes a new noise every week. I've stopped taking it to the mechanic. I just give each one a name and turn up the radio.
posts.caption: There's a click that only happens when I turn left. There's a hum that starts around forty miles an hour and stops right before the bank. And as of last Tuesday, there's a squeal that sounds exactly like my old boss when the copier jammed, so that one's named Gary. I took it in once in the spring. The mechanic drove it around the block, came back, and said he didn't hear anything. Then he charged me sixty dollars for the quiet. Now I keep a little notebook in the glove box. Every new noise gets a name and a date. Then I turn up the oldies station and we all ride together.
posts.first: My daughter rode with me on Sunday and asked what that rattling was. I said that's Linda, she comes and goes. My daughter didn't laugh. She looked up a shop on her phone and sent me the address. I wrote it down in the notebook, right under Linda.

posts.caption: It was a ten. One ten-dollar bill, handed over for paper towels, cereal, and a bottle of red that was on sale. The girl at the register lifted it up to the ceiling light and squinted at it like she was checking an X-ray. Then she ran the little marker over it. Then she looked at me. I'm fifty-six years old and wearing house shoes I forgot to change out of. If I had a printing press in my basement, I'd be at the good grocery store, the one with the olive bar. I got my change. She got a look she'll remember.
posts.first: My sister was behind me in line and swears I said it out loud. I maintain I only thought it very loudly. Either way the manager wandered over to see what the holdup was, looked at the bill, looked at me, and said have a nice day. I did, eventually.
posts.quote: I hate when cashiers hold my money up to the light to see if it’s real. Karen, if I could make counterfeit cash, I wouldn’t be shopping at the dollar store.

posts.quote: I can't believe it's almost November. I still haven't finished being annoyed about July.
posts.first: In July somebody at the gas station took the pump I was clearly pulling up to, and I thought about it all the way home. I'm still thinking about it. Meanwhile the leaves have changed, the clocks are about to fall back, and I've barely started on August.

posts.quote: My makeup bag has fourteen lipsticks. I wear the same one every day. The other thirteen belong to a Saturday-night version of me who hasn't been out since 2019.
posts.caption: I cleaned out my makeup bag on Sunday because I couldn't zip it anymore. Fourteen lipsticks. I lined them up on the bathroom counter like suspects. There's a red called Midnight Affair that I bought for a wedding in 2018. There's a plum one a girl at the mall talked me into. There's a coral I've never even opened. And then there's the one I actually wear, the same soft rose, every single day, worn down to a nub that I have to dig out with my pinky. I put all fourteen back in the bag. I'm not getting rid of her. She might go out again.
posts.first: My best friend saw the bag last weekend and grabbed the red one. She said wear this on Friday, we're going to dinner. I said fine. Friday came and I wore the soft rose. She noticed right away. She didn't say a word, just raised her glass like she'd expected it.

posts.quote: My neighbor already has eleven inflatables up for Halloween. I have one pumpkin on the step, and honestly, it looks tired too.
posts.caption: He started on the first of October. Saturday morning, ladder out, extension cords everywhere, his wife holding a coffee and pointing. By lunch there was a ghost taller than his garage. By Sunday there was a cat, a pumpkin with a top hat, a skeleton on a motorcycle and something I think is a witch, though it falls over every time the wind picks up. I count eleven. I sit on my porch most evenings and watch them inflate at six o'clock, one after another, like a slow parade. I have one pumpkin. It's on the step. It's leaning a little. We understand each other.
posts.first: The power went out on our street for twenty minutes Saturday night. Every single one of his inflatables sighed down at the same time and lay in the yard like a crime scene. I watched from my chair with my one pumpkin. Mine never even moved. Low maintenance has its rewards.

posts.quote: If you ask me how I'm doing, I'm going to tell you. All of it. That's the risk you took.
posts.caption: It was the neighborhood potluck at the community center on Sunday, right by the deviled eggs. Barbara from two doors down touched my arm and said so how are you doing. She meant it kindly. I could tell by the head tilt. So I told her. The knee, the furnace, the new neighbors with the leaf blower, the insurance company and the forty minutes on hold, my son's girlfriend, the price of eggs. About halfway through, she set down her plate. By the end she was nodding very slowly. Then she said well, goodness, and went to stand by the coffee. She asked. That's all I'm saying.
posts.first: At the next potluck, Barbara walked right up to me, smiled, and said nice to see you. Not how are you. Nice to see you. She's learned. I respect a woman who can adjust. I brought her a deviled egg as a peace offering and she took two.
